UNH.rationale: UNH presents a rare full-alignment negative case across all three pillars. Pillar 1 (fundamentals): The franchise is durable but deteriorating — net margin has halved from 5.6% to 2.8%, ROE collapsed from 22.8% to 12.3%, and revenue growth is a tepid +2.0% YoY. Membership is declining across all UnitedHealthcare segments (down ~1.5M since year-end 2025), Optum revenues contracted YoY, and management itself acknowledges margin recovery will extend past 2027 due to sticky commercial medical cost trends running above 11%. The Q2 2026 earnings beat ($6.38 vs $4.90 consensus) is real but achieved through repricing and book pruning, not organic growth — the franchise has shifted from 'growth compounder' to 'margin defender.' Pillar 2 (valuation): PE diluted sits at 30.08x, the very top of its 365-day range (9.5–31.0x), having nearly tripled from 11.15x a year ago while EPS grew only +0.7% YoY. P/B at 3.71x is also at its ceiling. Earnings yield of 3.3% is below the 10-year Treasury yield of 4.71%, meaning the market is paying more for each dollar of UNH earnings than for risk-free income. This valuation expansion has occurred against a backdrop of sharply deteriorating profitability — a dangerous disconnect. Pillar 3 (near-term catalyst): The DOJ antitrust investigation targeting the UnitedHealthcare-Optum vertical integration is a binary downside risk that could structurally challenge the premium multiple. Berkshire Hathaway's full exit of its 5M+ share position signals institutional skepticism. The combination of structural membership decline, regulatory overhang, margin headwinds extending past 2027, and an extreme valuation creates a strongly negative risk/reward skew.

Greg Abel, Berkshire Hathaway's new CEO, sold the company's entire 5 million+ share position in UnitedHealth Group earlier this year … At 23x forward earnings, the stock is reasonably priced … though not an absolute steal.
